summary:
The documented exposure points for transgender travellers in France are detention and the border. In accommodation, services and public movement, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition, and the Défenseur des droits has issued a framework decision with official guidance for service providers in response.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and accounts collected in a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

France's national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 and, in an opinion of 25 May 2021, found serious and persistent violations including placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure to strip-searches. It reported no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty. The national preventive mechanism explained in an APT interview that the new opinion was issued because the 2010 opinion produced no measurable change, that gender-recognition law and terminology had shifted, and that coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees; it cited structural problems of isolating vulnerable people and of suicide prevention, built on a decade of letters from detained trans people.

The placement issue remains live. On 4 February 2025, 20 Minutes reported that Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, had been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October, confirming that in 2025 trans detainees are still placed in facilities matching birth sex and that isolation is the management response. A deputy raised her case in oral question no. 219 to the Keeper of the Seals in the National Assembly, arguing that her incarceration exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees.

At the border, a first-person account published by StreetPress on 7 March 2017 describes trans woman Giovanna Rincon being publicly questioned for ten minutes by French border police at an airport in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction at French entry points for trans travellers.

The Défenseur des droits' framework decision on trans rights confirms persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony, cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey finding that 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and issues official guidance for service providers. Since 2017, transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and the December 2004 law extending the 1881 Freedom of the Press law covers incitement to hatred or violence and discrimination, with penalties increased where assault or murder is motivated by the victim's sexual orientation.

Gender-affirming healthcare carries documented access barriers. A 2022 ILGA-Europe report found lack of self-determination, extended waiting times, and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent model. Transsexualism is covered under ALD 31 with treatment funded by Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979, but trans rights organisations said the 2010 decree removing gender identity disorder as a diagnosis changed nothing in practice. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an "epidemic-like phenomenon" and a "primarily social problem" and advised extreme caution, though this did not change actual practice.

Marriage equality took effect in May 2013, with France's first same-sex wedding reported by CNN on 29 May 2013, establishing the legal baseline for partner recognition. The Court of Cassation ruled in December 2019 that foreign birth certificates recognising same-sex partners must be fully recognised in France.

Official hostility markers sit alongside the protection machinery. In March 2024, centre-right Republican senators commissioned The Little Mermaid Observatory, a group opposed to all forms of gender transition for minors, to report on youth gender-affirming care, which called such care a "health scandal" and youth transness a "social contagion"; the resulting bill to ban medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, provoking large-scale protests, but is opposed by the Macron government and has had no update since 23 July 2024. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, the interministerial body fighting anti-LGBT hatred, was a member of The Little Mermaid Observatory, which had called gender-affirming healthcare "mutilation"; one committee member resigned and the president stepped away. In late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for medical care of trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 alongside calcium and vitamin D.

A report released on 16 May 2020 showed homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against around 1,380 in 2018; in October 2018 President Macron denounced the violence as "unworthy of France" and promised unspecified "concrete measures". French law contains no visa, asylum or border-entry provision specific to LGBTQ people.

In higher education, Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced in March 2019 that all institutions must use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms. Conversion therapy was banned effective 1 February 2022, punishable by two years' imprisonment and/or a €30,000 fine.
tangentialFactors:
Acceptance figures for homosexuality, not trans identity, sit high in metropolitan France: a 2013 Pew Research Center survey found 77% of the French population believed homosexuality should be accepted, one of the highest of 39 countries polled, with 81% acceptance among 18–29 year-olds; the 2019 Eurobarometer found 79% backed same-sex marriage and 85% believed LGBT people should have equal rights, and the 2023 Eurobarometer found 79% and 84% respectively. These measure attitudes to sexual orientation, not to trans people, and the Défenseur des droits' citation of the 2023 EU Fundamental Rights Agency survey showing 64% of trans people in France reporting identity-related discrimination points the other way.

Acceptance is markedly lower overseas: a 2014 study found about 20% of overseas residents saw homosexuality as a sexuality like any other against 77% in metropolitan France, with Mayotte particularly taboo and the first same-sex marriages in Saint Martin and French Polynesia triggering public demonstrations. Mayotte sees frequent reports of family rejection, harassment and discrimination, and a 2006 Lifou Island proposal for a "family code" envisaged eviction or lynching of LGBTQ people; it was not approved.

Historical legal context: French law decriminalised sodomy in the Penal Code of 1791. A 1960 ordinance (the Mirguet amendment, article 330, 2nd alinea) doubled penalties for indecent exposure when homosexual in nature and remained in force until 1980. The Vichy government's 1942 article 334 set the age of consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual ones, equalised at 15 in 1982. In Alsace and Lorraine, LGBTQ people were persecuted and interned in concentration camps after the 1940 Nazi annexation. In March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for gay men arrested under Article 330 before 1980, still awaiting a Senate vote.

Public visibility markers: Gabriel Attal was one of the few openly gay heads of government in the world during his January–September 2024 premiership, and Paris Mayor Bertrand Delanoë came out publicly in 1998 before his 2001 election. Paris Pride drew 500,000 people in 2019, the city's third-largest event after the marathon and Techno Parade, and pride events now run in dozens of cities nationwide, with Le Marais, Quartier Pigalle and Bois de Boulogne hosting a thriving LGBTQ nightlife. Historically the National Assembly voted 293–222 against same-sex marriage in June 2011, and conservative outrage greeted the use of "parent 1" and "parent 2" on French school enrolment forms reported in February 2019.

A Women's Forum Australia report of August 2024 describes a Lyon hostel incident in which an Australian guest who objected to a man in the female dormitory bathroom was threatened with 'transphobia' by the manager, concerning sex-segregated accommodation in a French hostel.
localsOnly:
Resident-facing provisions: since 2017 transphobia has been an aggravating factor for all crimes punishable by prison, and LGBT people may serve openly in the French Armed Forces. The December 2004 law made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments illegal, carrying a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment; MP Christian Vanneste became the first person convicted under the law in January 2006, though the conviction was later cancelled by the Court of Cassation. Civil liberty groups including Reporters Without Borders criticised the law as a serious infringement on free speech, while the Chirac government cited rising anti-gay violence.

Healthcare and social provision: assisted reproduction for lesbian couples and single women took effect in September 2021 with state coverage for women under 43, and the MSM blood donation deferral was removed entirely on 16 March 2022. Intersex people retain significant gaps in protection from non-consensual medical interventions. France refused to recognise surrogate children as French citizens until 2015, leaving many in legal limbo.

Education policy: in March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos made fighting discrimination including homophobia one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009, and in January 2019 the Ministry of Education launched the campaign Tous égaux, tous alliés, which gives students reporting services and a helpline and requires all French schools to provide guidance about LGBTQ issues, with 17 May as a sensitisation day. In March 2019 Higher Education Minister Frédérique Vidal announced that all higher education institutions must use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms.

Youth care: in late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first guidelines for medical care of trans youth, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2 alongside calcium and vitamin D, while the Senate-passed under-18 transition ban bill of May 2024 remains pending with no update since 23 July 2024. The association Le Refuge estimated 3–4% of its helpline calls concerned conversion therapy before the 2022 ban.
outOfScopeNotes:
The CGLPL's figure of roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010 is a raw count of referrals received, not a rate, and the inventory provides no denominator for the trans detainee population, so its magnitude cannot be assessed.

The 36% rise in homophobic and transphobic attacks reported on 16 May 2020 covers 2019 against 2018 and combines homophobic and transphobic incidents without separating them; the inventory does not resolve whether trans-specific incidents rose at the same rate.

The inventory contains no trans-specific killing or violence rate for France, and no figure that could be compared against the general homicide rate; no such figure is asserted here.

The 20 Minutes report of 4 February 2025 on Louna and the National Assembly oral question are the most recent documented instances of trans prison placement in this inventory; no later case is documented.

The StreetPress account of border questioning dates from 7 March 2017; no later documented instance of identity-document friction at a French entry point appears in this inventory.

The Défenseur des droits framework decision is cited through its own announcement page; the full text and the precise obligations it places on service providers are not reproduced in the inventory.

Whether the CGLPL's binding guidance of 25 May 2021 has been implemented across establishments is unresolved in this inventory; the source records the guidance's issuance, not compliance outcomes.
